y-m-48-01.title: Find the wrong line in Minseo's checklist
y-m-48-01.topic: Converse, inverse, and contrapositive of a proposition, and judging true or false
y-m-48-01.goal: Tell the hypothesis and conclusion apart exactly, distinguish the converse, inverse, and contrapositive, and explain why a conclusion drawn from a wrongly built proposition cannot be trusted.
y-m-48-01.material: The universal set is all real numbers. Minseo checked the proposition p: 'If x>2, then x²>4' as shown below. (x² is read 'x squared'. '≤' means 'less than or equal to'.)
y-m-48-01.thinking.0: Find where the error starts in the working
y-m-48-01.thinking.1: Judge a false proposition using a counterexample
y-m-48-01.thinking.2: Pick out the proposition that has the same truth value as the original
y-m-48-01.prereq.0: School sequence assumption: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied middle school math (algebraic expressions, linear inequalities) and the basic set terms of high school Common Math (subset, union, intersection, complement, number of elements).
y-m-48-01.prereq.1: Tell the hypothesis and the conclusion apart in a proposition p→q
y-m-48-01.prereq.2: Look at the solution of the inequality x²>4 on a number line or by plugging in values
y-m-48-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line in Minseo's checking process.
y-m-48-01.s.s1.line.0: p: If x>2, then x²>4. If x>2, then x is positive and x·x>2·2, so p is true.
y-m-48-01.s.s1.line.1: Converse of p: If x²>4, then x>2.
y-m-48-01.s.s1.line.2: Contrapositive of p: If x≤2, then x²≤4.
y-m-48-01.s.s1.line.3: If x=−3, then x≤2 but x²=9>4, so this proposition is false.
y-m-48-01.s.s1.line.4: An original proposition and its contrapositive have the same truth value. Therefore p is false.
y-m-48-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is where the problem starts. 'If x≤2, then x²≤4' is the proposition (the inverse) made by only negating the hypothesis and the conclusion each, while the contrapositive makes the negation of the conclusion the hypothesis and the negation of the hypothesis the conclusion: 'If x²≤4, then x≤2'. This is why the conclusion in line 5 is also wrong. Line 1 already showed that p is true, and the correct contrapositive 'If x²≤4, then x≤2' is true. The calculation in line 4 (x=−3) is correct for the wrongly built proposition.
y-m-48-01.s.s2.prompt: Even if p is true, the converse of p can be false. Enter two different real numbers x that show the converse 'If x²>4, then x>2' is false.
y-m-48-01.s.s2.hint.0: Split the x that satisfy the converse's hypothesis x²>4 into positive and negative, and write a few of each.
y-m-48-01.s.s2.hint.1: For each value you wrote, check whether the conclusion x>2 holds, and pick the values where it does not.
y-m-48-01.s.s2.ok.c1: x² is greater than 4, so the converse's hypothesis holds.
y-m-48-01.s.s2.fail.c1: x² is not greater than 4. The converse's hypothesis does not hold, so this value cannot be a counterexample.
y-m-48-01.s.s2.ok.c2: x is 2 or less, so the converse's conclusion 'x>2' does not hold.
y-m-48-01.s.s2.fail.c2: x is greater than 2. The conclusion 'x>2' holds, so this is not a counterexample.
y-m-48-01.s.s2.explain: x²>4 holds when x>2 or x<−2. Values with x<−2 (for example −3, −2.5, −5) satisfy the hypothesis and break the conclusion, so the converse is false.
y-m-48-01.s.s3.r.d: A contrapositive always has the same truth value as the original proposition. First sort out which one is the contrapositive.
y-m-48-01.s.s1.hint.0: Divide p and the lines made from its converse, inverse, and contrapositive into two boxes each, "hypothesis → conclusion," and write them down.
y-m-48-01.s.s1.hint.1: Mark and compare how each line changed the hypothesis and conclusion of p (kept as is / swapped places / negated).
y-m-48-01.s.s3.prompt: The new proposition q: "If x is a multiple of 6, then x is a multiple of 3" (x is an integer) is true. Among the converse, inverse, and contrapositive of q, which one can be immediately said to be true from the truth of q alone?
y-m-48-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write q, the converse, the inverse, and the contrapositive in "hypothesis → conclusion" boxes, and mark which of them changes the boxes of q and how.
y-m-48-01.s.s3.hint.1: For the ones you suspect to be true, plug in values such as 3, 6, 9 and test that no counterexample appears.
y-m-48-01.s.s3.o.a: Inverse of q: If x is not a multiple of 6, then x is not a multiple of 3
y-m-48-01.s.s3.r.a: x=3 is a counterexample. 3 is not a multiple of 6, but it is a multiple of 3. This is independent of the truth of the original proposition.
y-m-48-01.s.s3.o.b: Contrapositive of q: If x is not a multiple of 3, then x is not a multiple of 6
y-m-48-01.s.s3.o.c: Converse of q: If x is a multiple of 3, then x is a multiple of 6
y-m-48-01.s.s3.r.c: x=3 is a counterexample. 3 is a multiple of 3 but not a multiple of 6. Even if the original proposition is true, the truth of the converse must be examined separately.
y-m-48-01.s.s3.o.d: For the converse, inverse, and contrapositive, none can be asserted to be true from q alone
y-m-48-01.s.s3.explain: A contrapositive always has the same truth value as the original proposition, so if q is true, the contrapositive "If x is not a multiple of 3, then x is not a multiple of 6" is also true. The converse and the inverse must be checked separately from q, and in this case x=3 is a counterexample, so both are false.

y-m-48-02.title: What kind of condition is 'x=2' for 'x²=4'?
y-m-48-02.topic: Necessary and sufficient conditions, and the effect of the universal set
y-m-48-02.goal: Explain with counterexamples and truth sets that judging a necessary or sufficient condition can change with the universal set, and make another condition with the same meaning.
y-m-48-02.material: Condition p: x²=4, condition q: x=2. The relationship between the two conditions can change with the universal set (the range of numbers x can be), so check the universal set every time. (x²=4 is read 'x squared equals 4', and |x|=2 is read 'the absolute value of x is 2'.)
y-m-48-02.thinking.0: Judge the relationship of conditions with truth sets
y-m-48-02.thinking.1: Revise a judgment according to new information (a change of universal set)
y-m-48-02.thinking.2: Explain with a counterexample why something is not a necessary condition
y-m-48-02.prereq.0: School sequence assumption: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied middle school math (algebraic expressions, linear inequalities) and the basic set terms of high school Common Math (subset, union, intersection, complement, number of elements).
y-m-48-02.prereq.1: Meaning of a truth set and the subset relation
y-m-48-02.prereq.2: Truth or falsity of the proposition 'if ..., then ...' and counterexamples
y-m-48-02.s.s1.prompt: Follow how the judgment changes each time the universal set and the conditions change.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write down all the x that satisfy p and all the x that satisfy q within the universal set.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the two groups: does one fit entirely inside the other, or are they equal?
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.0.info: The universal set is all real numbers. Condition p: x²=4, condition q: x=2.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: What kind of condition is q for p? (Check separately whether 'if q then p' and whether 'if p then q'.)
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.0.after: If x=2, then x²=4, so 'if q then p' is true. But x=−2 satisfies p and does not satisfy q, so 'if p then q' is false. So q is a sufficient condition for p, but not a necessary condition.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A necessary condition but not quite a sufficient condition
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: First check whether 'if q then p' holds. What happens when you put x=2 into p?
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: A sufficient condition but not a necessary condition
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment made by noticing that 'if q then p' is true and 'if p then q' is false.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Check whether 2 is the only x that satisfies p.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Did you check whether 'if q then p' holds? Put x=2 into p.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Now shrink the universal set to 'all positive real numbers'. p: x²=4 and q: x=2 stay the same.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: In this universal set, what kind of condition is q for p?
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.1.after: Among the positive real numbers, 2 is the only x with x²=4, so the truth set of p and the truth set of q are equal. So in this universal set it is a necessary and sufficient condition. Even with the same conditions, the judgment can change when the universal set changes.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: A sufficient condition but not a necessary condition
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You kept your first judgment unchanged. Write how the group of x that satisfy p changes when the universal set shrinks.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: A necessary condition but not a sufficient condition
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Start by checking whether 'if q then p' holds. In this universal set too, x=2 satisfies p.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You judged this by seeing that the group of x satisfying p and the group of x satisfying q are the same.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The universal set changed, so it cannot be judged
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Once the universal set is fixed, you can judge it. Write all the x that satisfy p and q within it.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Return the universal set to all real numbers. This time, keep p as it is and change q to another condition so that it becomes a necessary and sufficient condition for p.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: Choose a condition that can replace q. (More than one may be correct.)
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.2.after: The truth set of p is {−2, 2}. Both |x|=2 and 'x=2 or x=−2' are exactly this set, so they are necessary and sufficient conditions and are different expressions with the same meaning. x>0 leaves out −2, and x²≥4 lets in more values such as 3.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: It includes only x=2 and leaves out x=−2. Compare it with the truth set {−2, 2} of p.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It includes both x=2 and x=−2, so it becomes equal to the truth set of p.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: It includes all the x that satisfy p, but it also contains values like x=3 that do not satisfy p.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a judgment that copies the truth set {−2, 2} of p as it is.
y-m-48-02.s.s1.reflect: The reason the judgment changed in step 2 is not that the conditions changed but that the universal set changed. In your own words, sum up that the same condition can have a different truth set depending on the universal set. How can the way q was changed in step 3 be explained with truth sets?
y-m-48-02.s.s2.prompt: Explain, using one specific value of x, why you can say 'x=2 is not a necessary condition for x²=4' when the universal set is all real numbers.
y-m-48-02.s.s2.hint.0: Sort out and write which is false in the sentence: 'if p then q' or 'if q then p'.
y-m-48-02.s.s2.hint.1: Write all the x that satisfy p, and look for any of them that do not satisfy q.
y-m-48-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is it clear that p is true and q is false for the value you chose?
y-m-48-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write the link that since 'if p then q' is false, q is not a necessary condition?
y-m-48-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid mixing up the directions of necessary and sufficient?
y-m-48-02.s.s2.model.0: If x=−2, then x²=4, so p holds, but x is not 2, so q does not hold. So 'if p then q' is false, and q is not a necessary condition for p.
y-m-48-02.s.s2.model.1: The values that satisfy p include −2 as well as 2. There is a case where x²=4 but x≠2, so we cannot say q is a necessary condition for p.

y-m-48-03.title: Find the value of a that makes a sufficient condition
y-m-48-03.topic: Inclusion of truth sets and the range of the letter a
y-m-48-03.goal: Turn a sufficient condition into an inclusion of truth sets, make several possible values of the letter a, and explain how including or excluding the endpoints affects the range.
y-m-48-03.material: There are two conditions about a real number x. p: −1≤x≤2, q: |x−a|≤3 (a is a real number). We want to choose a so that 'if p then q' is true. (|x−a| is read 'the absolute value of x minus a'. |x−a|≤3 means x is at most 3 away from a.)
y-m-48-03.thinking.0: Translate a sufficient condition into an inclusion of truth sets
y-m-48-03.thinking.1: Make several solutions that satisfy the constraint
y-m-48-03.thinking.2: Compare ranges depending on whether the endpoints are included
y-m-48-03.prereq.0: School sequence assumption: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied middle school math (algebraic expressions, linear inequalities) and the basic set terms of high school Common Math (subset, union, intersection, complement, number of elements).
y-m-48-03.prereq.1: Rewrite the absolute value inequality |x−a|≤3 as an interval
y-m-48-03.prereq.2: Look at the inclusion of intervals on a number line
y-m-48-03.s.s1.prompt: When 'if p then q' is true, what does that mean about P and Q, the groups of x (truth sets) that satisfy p and q?
y-m-48-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write in words what x would be needed for 'if p then q' to be false.
y-m-48-03.s.s1.hint.1: Test the sentence with small groups like P={1, 2}, Q={1, 2, 3} to see whether it fits.
y-m-48-03.s.s1.o.a: Every x in Q is also in P
y-m-48-03.s.s1.r.a: The direction is reversed. 'If p then q' means that if p is satisfied, q is satisfied too.
y-m-48-03.s.s1.o.b: There is at least one x that is in both P and Q
y-m-48-03.s.s1.r.b: Overlapping in at least one place is different from every x of P being inside Q. If there is an x in P that is not in Q, it is a counterexample.
y-m-48-03.s.s1.o.c: Every x in P is also in Q
y-m-48-03.s.s1.o.d: P and Q have the same number of x
y-m-48-03.s.s1.r.d: Having the same number does not make the groups equal or make one fit inside the other.
y-m-48-03.s.s1.explain: 'If p then q' being true means every x that satisfies p also satisfies q, so P⊂Q.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.prompt: Enter 4 different real numbers a that make p: −1≤x≤2 a sufficient condition for q: |x−a|≤3. They do not have to be integers.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.hint.0: Rewrite |x−a|≤3 as a range (interval) of x, and draw it on a number line together with P.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.hint.1: Pick a value for a and check whether both endpoints −1 and 2 of P are inside the range of q.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The left end a−3 of q is −1 or less, so it covers up to the left end of P.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The left end a−3 of q is greater than −1, so part of the left side of P is outside q.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The right end a+3 of q is 2 or more, so it covers up to the right end of P.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The right end a+3 of q is less than 2, so part of the right side of P is outside q.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.explain: q is a−3≤x≤a+3. For P={x | −1≤x≤2} to fit entirely inside Q, we need a−3≤−1 and 2≤a+3, so −1≤a≤2. Every value in this range is a correct answer.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.because.prompt: If a=3, then p is not a sufficient condition for q. Explain why by giving one actual value of x in P.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put a=3 into the expression for q and write q as an interval of x.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Find and write one x in P that is not in the interval of q.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.because.placeholder: e.g., If a=3, the range of q is ..., and x=... is ...
y-m-48-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does the x you chose really belong to P (from −1 to 2)?
y-m-48-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you find the range of q for a=3 and compare it with that x?
y-m-48-03.s.s2.because.model.0: If a=3, then q is 0≤x≤6. x=−1 in P is not in q, so there is an x that is p but not q, and it is not a sufficient condition.
y-m-48-03.s.s2.because.model.1: If a=3, then q is from 0 to 6, but values like −1, the left end of p, or −0.5 are outside this range. So 'if p then q' does not hold.
y-m-48-03.s.s3.prompt: Keep p as −1≤x≤2 and change q to |x−a|<3 (no equals sign). Which is the range of a that makes p a sufficient condition for q?
y-m-48-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write q as an interval for a=−1 and a=2 and check whether the endpoints of P are inside.
y-m-48-03.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the boundary values a=−1 and a=2 with an inside value a=0.
y-m-48-03.s.s3.r.a: You treated it the same as the case that includes the endpoints. If a=2, then q is −1<x<5, so check whether x=−1 in P belongs to it.
y-m-48-03.s.s3.r.b: Check the case a=2. q: −1<x<5, and P has x=−1.
y-m-48-03.s.s3.r.c: Check the case a=−1. q: −4<x<2, and P has x=2.
y-m-48-03.s.s3.explain: Both endpoints −1 and 2 of P belong to P, but this Q does not include its endpoints. So we need a−3<−1 and 2<a+3, and therefore −1<a<2.

y-m-48-04.title: Test the saying 'if the square is bigger, it is bigger'
y-m-48-04.topic: Counterexamples and the extra condition that makes a proposition hold
y-m-48-04.goal: Make a counterexample to a false proposition yourself, find several extra conditions that make the proposition hold, and explain why using signs and squares.
y-m-48-04.material: For real numbers a and b, Hyunwoo said, "'If a²>b², then a>b' is true. It works when a=3, b=2 and it also worked when a=5, b=1." (a² is read 'a squared'.)
y-m-48-04.thinking.1: Compare and evaluate several ways to fix it
y-m-48-04.thinking.2: Explain the reason for the fixing condition
y-m-48-04.prereq.0: School sequence assumption: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied middle school math (algebraic expressions, linear inequalities) and the basic set terms of high school Common Math (subset, union, intersection, complement, number of elements).
y-m-48-04.prereq.1: Properties of inequalities and the meaning of absolute value
y-m-48-04.prereq.2: Counterexample of a proposition (an example where the hypothesis holds and the conclusion does not)
y-m-48-04.s.s1.prompt: Enter three different ordered pairs (a, b) that show Hyunwoo's proposition 'If a²>b², then a>b' is false. (a and b are real numbers.)
y-m-48-04.s.s1.hint.0: You need a pair where the hypothesis holds and the conclusion does not. Pick some a and b and first compare a² and b².
y-m-48-04.s.s1.hint.1: Test whether a counterexample appears when a and b are both positive, then also try cases where the signs differ and where both are negative.
y-m-48-04.s.s1.ok.c1: a² is greater than b², so the hypothesis holds.
y-m-48-04.s.s1.fail.c1: a² is not greater than b². The hypothesis must hold for it to be a counterexample.
y-m-48-04.s.s1.ok.c2: a>b does not hold, so the conclusion fails.
y-m-48-04.s.s1.fail.c2: a>b holds. The conclusion is right, so this is not a counterexample.
y-m-48-04.s.s1.explain: The hypothesis a²>b² means the same as |a|>|b|. If a is negative and has the larger absolute value, like (−3, 1), then a²>b² but a<b, so it is a counterexample. Using only positive numbers gives no counterexample.
y-m-48-04.s.s2.prompt: We want to add one condition so that Hyunwoo's proposition becomes true. Choose all the conditions that make the proposition always true when added. (a and b are real numbers.)
y-m-48-04.s.s2.hint.0: Apply each condition to the counterexample pairs you made in the first step and check whether the counterexample still remains under that condition.
y-m-48-04.s.s2.hint.1: Try making pairs yourself where a is 0 or more, a²>b², and a≤b, and test whether that is possible.
y-m-48-04.s.s2.o.a: b is 0 or more and a is any real number
y-m-48-04.s.s2.r.a: (−3, 1) is still a counterexample under this condition. Even if b is 0 or more, a can be negative.
y-m-48-04.s.s2.o.c: a and b are different real numbers
y-m-48-04.s.s2.r.c: (−3, 1) is a counterexample even though they are different real numbers.
y-m-48-04.s.s2.o.d: a and b are both positive
y-m-48-04.s.s2.o.e: a and b are both integers
y-m-48-04.s.s2.r.e: (−3, 1) is a pair of integers. The condition of being integers does not solve the problem of signs.
y-m-48-04.s.s2.explain: If a≥0, then from a²>b² we get a=|a|>|b|≥b, so it is true. The condition that a and b are both positive is stronger than that, so it is also true. For all the others, (−3, 1) remains as a counterexample.
y-m-48-04.s.s2.acc.0: The condition that a is 0 or more is enough on its own to make the proposition true. But you missed that the condition 'a and b are both positive' is also sufficient.
y-m-48-04.s.s2.acc.1: The condition that a and b are both positive is sufficient. You missed that the weaker condition 'a is 0 or more' alone also makes the proposition true.
y-m-48-04.s.s3.prompt: Explain why the added condition is needed and what changes when you square, focusing on those points.
y-m-48-04.s.s3.hint.0: For (−3, 1), compare a² and b², and a and b, and write what is different.
y-m-48-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write how a and |a| are related when a is 0 or more.
y-m-48-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say that squaring loses the information about signs?
y-m-48-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect why a condition like a≥0 blocks the counterexample?
y-m-48-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you test your explanation with (−3, 1)?
y-m-48-04.s.s3.model.0: Squaring removes the sign of a negative number, so there are cases like a=−3, b=1 where the square is bigger but a is smaller. That is why the condition that a is 0 or more is needed.
y-m-48-04.s.s3.model.1: a²>b² means |a|>|b|, so it compares only sizes (absolute values). If a can be negative, a>b may not hold, so a condition like a≥0 must be added.

y-m-48-05.prereq.1: Number of elements of a finite set (how to count the elements of a union)
y-m-48-05.prereq.2: Move a Venn diagram into a table
y-m-48-05.s.s1.prompt: From the data known now (40 students in total, 18 in the reading club, 15 in the coding club) alone, can we determine exactly how many students joined neither club?
y-m-48-05.s.s1.hint.0: Put the students who joined only A, only B, and both separately, and write who is included in 18 and in 15.
y-m-48-05.s.s1.hint.1: Assume the overlap is 0 students and 5 students, calculate the number of students who did not join in each case, and compare.
y-m-48-05.s.s1.r.a: A student who joined both clubs is included in both 18 and 15. Check whether these students were counted twice.
y-m-48-05.s.s1.o.b: It cannot be determined. We would need to know the grades of all 40 students
y-m-48-05.s.s1.r.b: Grades are information unrelated to whether a student joined. Find what is missing in the relationship among the numbers.
y-m-48-05.s.s1.o.c: It cannot be determined. It depends on the number of students who joined both
y-m-48-05.s.s1.o.d: 20 students. Because there are two clubs, so 40 is halved
y-m-48-05.s.s1.r.d: Dividing students by the number of clubs does not give the number of students who did not join. Start by working out the number who joined.
y-m-48-05.s.s1.explain: The number of students who joined is n(A)+n(B)−n(A∩B)=33−n(A∩B). If we do not know the number of overlapping students n(A∩B), the number of students who did not join, 40−(33−n(A∩B)), is not determined either.
y-m-48-05.s.s2.prompt: Let's make possible cases. Enter 3 different pairs (k, n), where k is the number of students who joined both clubs and n is the number who joined neither, that do not conflict with the data.
y-m-48-05.s.s2.hint.0: Start with the case where 0 students overlap, and first find the number of students who joined.
y-m-48-05.s.s2.hint.1: Increase k one at a time and write a table, then check where the largest value k can take gets blocked.
y-m-48-05.s.s2.var.k: Number of students who joined both k
y-m-48-05.s.s2.var.n: Number of students who joined neither n
y-m-48-05.s.s2.ok.c1: k is an integer from 0 to 15 (it cannot be more than the 15 students of the coding club).
y-m-48-05.s.s2.fail.c1: k must be an integer that is 0 or more and at most 15, the number of coding club members.
y-m-48-05.s.s2.fail.c2: n is different from 40−(number of students who joined). The number who joined is 18+15−k.
y-m-48-05.s.s2.ok.c3: n is an integer that is 0 or more.
y-m-48-05.s.s2.fail.c3: n must be an integer that is 0 or more.
y-m-48-05.s.s2.explain: The number of students who joined is 18+15−k=33−k, so n=40−(33−k)=7+k. k can be 0 to 15, so every integer from 7 to 22 is possible for n. The data alone does not fix a single value.
y-m-48-05.s.s3.prompt: Choose all the pieces of information such that, if just that one were given, we could know exactly how many students joined neither club.
y-m-48-05.s.s3.hint.0: Turn each piece of information into an equation using k, and check whether the value of k is fixed to a single value.
y-m-48-05.s.s3.hint.1: For information that does not fix it, make one example where that information still holds while the value of k is different.
y-m-48-05.s.s3.o.a: Number of students who joined only the reading club
y-m-48-05.s.s3.o.b: Number of students in the coding club who wear glasses
y-m-48-05.s.s3.r.b: Wearing glasses has nothing to do with the overlap of the two clubs. The information must fix the number of overlapping students.
y-m-48-05.s.s3.o.c: Number of students who joined both clubs
y-m-48-05.s.s3.o.d: The fact that 7 or more students did not join
y-m-48-05.s.s3.r.d: We already confirmed in an earlier step that it is 7 or more. It fixes no new value, so several possible values remain.
y-m-48-05.s.s3.o.e: Number of students who joined at least one club
y-m-48-05.s.s3.explain: Information that fixes the number of overlapping students k is enough. 'The number who joined only A' is 18−k and 'the number who joined at least one' is 33−k, so we can find k. '7 or more' only tells us k≥0 and does not fix k.
y-m-48-05.s.s4.prompt: The student council president said, 'Only 5 students have joined neither club.' What can we say about this statement from the data so far?
y-m-48-05.s.s4.hint.0: In the table you made in the earlier step, find the smallest value of n.
y-m-48-05.s.s4.hint.1: Check in the table whether n gets bigger or smaller as k gets bigger.
y-m-48-05.s.s4.o.a: It cannot be. Even with the least overlap, at least 7 do not join
y-m-48-05.s.s4.o.b: We cannot know. We do not know the number of overlapping students, so any value is possible
y-m-48-05.s.s4.r.b: Even without knowing the number of overlapping students, we can fix the range of possible values. Look at the values n can take in the earlier table.
y-m-48-05.s.s4.o.c: It is possible. When many students overlap, fewer students do not join
y-m-48-05.s.s4.r.c: When more students overlap, the number who joined actually goes down. So the number who did not join goes up.
y-m-48-05.s.s4.o.d: It cannot be. 5 out of 40 feels too few
y-m-48-05.s.s4.r.d: You have to compare with the calculated range, not a feeling. Check the smallest value n can take.
y-m-48-05.s.s4.explain: n=7+k and k≥0, so n is 7 or more. Even without knowing the overlap, 5 is outside the range of possible values (7 to 22), so the statement cannot be right. Even when information is missing, we can judge which values are impossible.

y-m-48-06.title: What is the opposite of 'everyone likes it'?
y-m-48-06.goal: Make the negation of propositions that contain 'all' and 'or', and test a wrong negation with a class where p is true to reveal the error.
y-m-48-06.material: We surveyed 10 students in one class (the universal set U). M is the group of students who like math, and E is the group of students who like English. Proposition p: 'Every student likes math or English' (here 'or' includes the case of liking both). The negation of a proposition is a proposition that is false when the original is true and true when the original is false. Sua made the negation of p as shown below. (Mᶜ is read 'the complement of M', ∩ is intersection, ∪ is union, and ∅ is the empty set.)
y-m-48-06.thinking.1: Test with the definition of negation (the truth value is always opposite)
y-m-48-06.thinking.2: Build a configuration that serves as a counterexample
y-m-48-06.prereq.0: School sequence assumption: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied middle school math (algebraic expressions, linear inequalities) and the basic set terms of high school Common Math (subset, union, intersection, complement, number of elements).
y-m-48-06.prereq.1: Meaning of propositions that contain 'all' and 'some'
y-m-48-06.prereq.2: Meaning of the union M∪E, the complement, and the intersection
y-m-48-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose one wrong line in Sua's working.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.hint.0: Imagine a class with a mix of students who like only math, only English, and both, and check in each line whether it is true or false in that class.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.line.0: p: Every student belongs to M∪E. That is, M∪E=U.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.line.1: For the negation, change 'all' to 'some' and also negate the condition that follows.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.line.2: The negation of 'likes math or English' is 'does not like math or does not like English'.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.line.3: So the negation of p: Some student does not like math or does not like English.
y-m-48-06.s.s1.line.4: In terms of sets, it can be written as Mᶜ∪Eᶜ≠∅ (not the empty set).
y-m-48-06.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The negation of 'likes math or English' is 'likes neither math nor English' (negating 'or' gives 'and'). So lines 4 and 5 are wrong as well. The correct negation is 'Some student likes neither math nor English', and in terms of sets, Mᶜ∩Eᶜ≠∅. Lines 1 and 2 are correct.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.prompt: We want to show that Sua's negation (line 4) is not the exact opposite of p. Make 3 different classes in which p is true and yet Sua's negation is true. There are 10 students in all, and each likes at least one of math or English. m is the number who like only math, e is the number who like only English, and b is the number who like both.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.hint.0: First decide how many students who like neither would be needed for p to be true.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.hint.1: For each type of student (only math, only English, both), check whether there is a student who 'does not like math or does not like English'.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.var.m: Number of students who like only math m
y-m-48-06.s.s2.var.e: Number of students who like only English e
y-m-48-06.s.s2.var.b: Number of students who like both b
y-m-48-06.s.s2.ok.c1: All three numbers are integers that are 0 or more.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of students must be an integer that is 0 or more.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.ok.c2: All 10 students like at least one of the two, so p is true.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum is not 10. All 10 students must like at least one of the two for p to be true.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.ok.c3: There is a student who does not like one of math or English, so Sua's negation is true.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.fail.c3: All 10 students like both, so Sua's negation is false.
y-m-48-06.s.s2.explain: For example, if (m, e, b)=(5, 5, 0), all 10 students like one of the two, so p is true, and there are also students who do not like one of math or English, so Sua's negation is also true. A negation that is not false when p is true is not an exact negation.
y-m-48-06.s.s3.prompt: Which is the correct negation of p?
y-m-48-06.s.s3.hint.0: Using the class configurations from the earlier step, check whether each option is true when p is true, and eliminate the options that are true.
y-m-48-06.s.s3.o.a: Every student likes neither math nor English
y-m-48-06.s.s3.r.a: You left 'all' as it was. Even if only some students like neither, p is false.
y-m-48-06.s.s3.o.b: Some student does not like math or does not like English
y-m-48-06.s.s3.r.b: This is the negation Sua made. In the earlier step's (5, 5, 0), it is true at the same time as p.
y-m-48-06.s.s3.explain: p says that 'likes math or English' holds for every student, so its negation says there is at least one student for whom it does not hold. That student likes neither math nor English (Mᶜ∩Eᶜ≠∅).
y-m-48-06.s.s1.hint.1: In a class where p is true, the negation of p must be false. For each line, test whether it is true or false in such a class.
y-m-48-06.s.s3.hint.1: Make one class yourself in which p is false, and check which choices are true in that class.
y-m-48-06.s.s3.o.c: There is a student who likes neither math nor English
y-m-48-06.s.s3.o.d: Every student does not like math or does not like English
y-m-48-06.s.s3.r.d: It kept "every," and the negation of "or" is also wrong. Check the two parts separately.

y-m-48-07.title: If you check many examples, does it become a proof?
y-m-48-07.topic: Propositions with 'all', counterexamples, and the limits of checking examples
y-m-48-07.goal: See through step-by-step data that a 'for all n' proposition cannot be proved by checking some values and that one counterexample makes it false, and state the difference from an existence proposition.
y-m-48-07.material: Call the following proposition q. q: 'For every natural number n, n²+n+41 is a prime number.' (n² is read 'n squared'. A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself.) The data is revealed one piece at a time.
y-m-48-07.thinking.1: Adjust how sure you are to fit new data
y-m-48-07.thinking.2: Compare the role of examples in 'for all' and 'there exists' propositions
y-m-48-07.prereq.0: School sequence assumption: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied middle school math (algebraic expressions, linear inequalities) and the basic set terms of high school Common Math (subset, union, intersection, complement, number of elements).
y-m-48-07.prereq.1: Meaning of a prime number and testing for primes
y-m-48-07.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose your thought about q.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.hint.0: Tell apart whether the data at each step covers all natural numbers n or only some of them.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.hint.1: Do the calculation in the new data yourself and check that it matches the given values.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.info: When n=1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are substituted, n²+n+41 gives 43, 47, 53, 61, 71, and all of them are prime.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think about q now?
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.after: The five results are a clue that q may be true, but they do not cover 'every natural number n', so they are not a proof.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: All five are prime, so q has been proved
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Five is only some of all the natural numbers. We do not yet know whether it holds for n that we did not substitute.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Primes coming up one after another is a coincidence, so q is probably false
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Primes coming up one after another is a clue that supports q. Having a clue is no basis for declaring it false either.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: q may be true, but it has not been proved
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Five gives no information at all
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: It is a clue on the side of q being true. But the important point is that it is not a proof.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.info: A computer calculated everything from n=1 to 39, and all of them were prime.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: What will you do now? Choose the suitable actions. (More than one may be correct.)
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.after: Testing the next value directly (looking for a counterexample) and finding the reason it holds for every n (proving) are both suitable. Checking 39 values raises your belief but does not prove q.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.o.a: All 39 were right, so treat q as proved and stop
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Even 39 is only some of all the natural numbers. The number of values checked is not the standard for a proof.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Calculate the next values directly, such as n=40 and 41
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Look in the expression for the reason it is prime and try to explain it
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Think the 40th is likely to be right too, so there is no need to check any more
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Being likely is different from being true. A counterexample can appear at a value you have not yet checked.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: What can you say about q now?
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.after: When n=40, n²+n+41=41×41 is not prime, so q is false. One counterexample makes a 'for all n' proposition false. n=41 is also composite, so it cannot be fixed by removing just one exception.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is prime for most n, so treat q as almost true and use it as it is
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: A 'for all n' proposition is false if even one case fails. 'Most' is not what q says.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Fix it by removing only n=40 as an exception, 'if n is not 40, it is prime', and it is true
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: n=41 also gives 41²+41+41=41×43, which is composite. A proposition fixed by removing one exception must be tested again.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 1681 might be a calculation mistake, so put off the judgment
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You can check 41×41 by multiplying directly. A calculation you can check should be checked before you judge.
y-m-48-07.s.s1.st.2.o.d: q is false. n=40 is a counterexample
y-m-48-07.s.s1.reflect: How did your confidence in q change in steps 1, 2, and 3? Which information only raised your confidence, and which information ended the judgment itself? Write how that difference connects to the difference between 'there are many examples' and 'there is one example'.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.prompt: Let q' be 'there exists a natural number n for which n²+n+41 is a composite number (a number greater than 1 that is not prime)'. What can we say about q' from the information in step 3 alone?
y-m-48-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write in words what kind of n is needed for q' to be true, and check whether 40 satisfies that condition.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write side by side the role n=40 plays in q and in q', and compare.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.o.a: One n=40 is enough to settle that q' is true
y-m-48-07.s.s2.o.b: We must check more n to know whether it is true or false
y-m-48-07.s.s2.r.b: q' is an 'exists' proposition, so it is true once you find one example that satisfies the condition. Check whether 40 is such an example.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.o.c: It is false. Because primes come out for most n
y-m-48-07.s.s2.r.c: An 'exists' proposition asks whether there is even one example, not whether most are.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.o.d: It cannot be called true. The counterexample is about q, not q'
y-m-48-07.s.s2.r.d: The same value n=40 as the counterexample becomes an example that satisfies the condition in q'. Compare how the two propositions use the same value differently.
y-m-48-07.s.s2.explain: q, the 'for all n' proposition, becomes false with one counterexample, and q', the 'some n exists' proposition, becomes true with one example that satisfies the condition. On the other hand, to say q is true, checking any number of examples is not enough.
y-m-48-07.s.s3.prompt: A friend who checked that n=1 to 10 are all prime says, 'Proof done!' Write why it is still not enough and what to do next, so your friend is not disappointed.
y-m-48-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write side by side the range of n your friend checked and the range of n that q talks about, and compare.
y-m-48-07.s.s3.hint.1: Decide on one n to test next and write the reason in one line.
y-m-48-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you acknowledge your friend's effort while making it clear that proving and checking are different?
y-m-48-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you suggest concretely 'which value to test' or 'how to prove it'?
y-m-48-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you state the judgment accurately without declaring that q is false?
y-m-48-07.s.s3.model.0: Checking 10 values is a good start. But you only looked at some values, so it may not be prime for larger n. Let's plug in the next value like n=40 to look for a counterexample, or think about the reason it would hold for every n.
y-m-48-07.s.s3.model.1: Getting ten primes is only a clue that q might be right. We have not checked all natural numbers, so we need to calculate larger n or prove the reason.

y-m-48-08.title: Two friends' set equalities: who is right?
y-m-48-08.topic: Laws of set operations: difference sets and their relation to union and intersection
y-m-48-08.goal: Pick out a false equality using one example, find for yourself the types of elements that make it false, and design what to check in order to believe that an equality always holds.
y-m-48-08.material: A, B, and C are sets. A−B is 'the group of elements that belong to A but do not belong to B' (the difference set). Jimin says 'A−(B∪C)=(A−B)∪(A−C)' always holds, and Doyun says 'A−(B∪C)=(A−B)∩(A−C)' always holds. (∪ is union and ∩ is intersection.)
y-m-48-08.thinking.0: Judge an equality false using one counterexample
y-m-48-08.thinking.1: Split into cases by the type of membership of an element
y-m-48-08.thinking.2: Design a sufficient way to check
y-m-48-08.prereq.0: School sequence assumption: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied middle school math (algebraic expressions, linear inequalities) and the basic set terms of high school Common Math (subset, union, intersection, complement, number of elements).
y-m-48-08.prereq.1: Meaning of difference set, union, and intersection
y-m-48-08.prereq.2: Think by splitting on whether an element belongs to a set or not
y-m-48-08.s.s1.prompt: You checked the two equalities with A={1, 2, 3, 4}, B={1, 2}, C={2, 3}. What is the most suitable thing we can learn from this example?
y-m-48-08.s.s1.hint.0: First find B∪C, A−B, and A−C separately.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.hint.1: Write the left and right sides of the three expressions side by side using the sets you found, and compare whether they are equal.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.o.a: Both equalities hold in this example, so both always hold
y-m-48-08.s.s1.r.a: Calculate both sides of Jimin's expression yourself and check whether they are equal. Even if it holds in one example, you cannot say it always holds.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.o.b: Doyun's equality held in this example, so it always holds, and Jimin's is false
y-m-48-08.s.s1.r.b: The judgment that Jimin's equality is false is right. But you cannot say Doyun's equality always holds just because it held in one example.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.o.c: This one example cannot decide the truth of either equality
y-m-48-08.s.s1.r.c: One example is enough to knock down 'it always holds'. Calculate what happens to Jimin's equality in this example.
y-m-48-08.s.s1.o.d: Jimin's equality is false. Doyun's equality only held in this example
y-m-48-08.s.s1.explain: In this example, A−(B∪C)={4} and (A−B)∪(A−C)={3, 4}∪{1, 4}={1, 3, 4}, so Jimin's equality breaks (false). Since (A−B)∩(A−C)={3, 4}∩{1, 4}={4}, Doyun's equality holds in this example, but it is only one example.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.prompt: Let's find the types of elements for which Jimin's equality breaks. Say an element x gets 1 if it belongs to a set among A, B, C and 0 if it does not, and write it as (a, b, c). Enter different (a, b, c) for which x belongs to only one of A−(B∪C) and (A−B)∪(A−C).
y-m-48-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write what x not belonging to B∪C means for B and C, and then write in order where x belongs among A−B and A−C.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.hint.1: Make a table of the 8 possible (a, b, c) and find the rows where the memberships of the two sides differ.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.ok.c1: a, b, and c are all 0 or 1.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.fail.c1: a, b, and c can only be 0 or 1.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.ok.c2: x belongs to only one of the two sets.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.fail.c2: x belongs to both sets or to neither. This is a type for which the equality does not break.
y-m-48-08.s.s2.explain: If (a, b, c)=(1, 1, 0), then x belongs to B∪C so it is not in A−(B∪C), but it does not belong to C so it is in A−C, and therefore it is in (A−B)∪(A−C). (1, 0, 1) is the same. If you make a set example that has even one such element, Jimin's equality breaks.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.prompt: What should you check to believe that Doyun's equality A−(B∪C)=(A−B)∩(A−C) always holds?
y-m-48-08.s.s3.hint.0: First count how many cases there are in all when an element is split by whether it belongs to A, B, and C or not.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.hint.1: Write both sides in words using 'belongs to' as the definition says, and compare whether they become the same sentence.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.o.a: Pick two or three more set examples and see whether both sides are equal
y-m-48-08.s.s3.r.a: Even with more examples, you have not checked 'all cases'. This kind of checking raises your belief but does not guarantee all cases.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.o.b: Shade just one region in a Venn diagram and see whether both sides are equal
y-m-48-08.s.s3.r.b: One region is only a part of the 8 cases.
y-m-48-08.s.s3.o.c: Check that the memberships of the two sides are the same in all 8 cases of (a, b, c)

y-m-48-09.title: If n² is even, is n even too?
y-m-48-09.topic: Proof using the contrapositive and comparing the validity of proofs
y-m-48-09.goal: Pick out which of three solutions can be accepted as a proof, explain to a middle school student why a proof using the contrapositive proves the original proposition, and tell apart propositions where the same method works from those where it does not.
y-m-48-09.material: Three students solved the proposition r: 'If n² is even, then n is even' for a natural number n in different ways. (n² is read 'n squared'. An even number can be written in the form 2k, and an odd number in the form 2k+1.)
y-m-48-09.thinking.0: Distinguish a proof from checking examples
y-m-48-09.thinking.1: Explain the logic of a proof using the contrapositive to someone else
y-m-48-09.thinking.2: Sort out the truth or falsity of propositions that look similar
y-m-48-09.prereq.0: School sequence assumption: 'H2' in this task is only a difficulty and support level in this production assignment; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Assume the learner has already studied middle school math (algebraic expressions, linear inequalities) and the basic set terms of high school Common Math (subset, union, intersection, complement, number of elements).
y-m-48-09.prereq.1: That an even number can be written as 2k and an odd number as 2k+1
y-m-48-09.prereq.2: The relation between a proposition's contrapositive and its truth value
y-m-48-09.s.s1.prompt: Three students say they proved r: 'When n is a natural number, if n² is even, then n is even.' Choose all the solutions that can be accepted as a proof that r is true.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.hint.0: Compare which values of n each of the three solutions deals with.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.hint.1: Write in one line each what Hajun and Jiyu assumed and what they drew as the conclusion, and compare with r.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.o.a: Seoa: I looked for all the cases from n=1 to 10 where n² is even, and they were n=2, 4, 6, 8, 10, all even. Therefore r is true.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.r.a: n=11 and above were not checked. Checking some values is not a proof.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.o.b: Jiyu: n²=n×n. I already know odd times odd is odd, so if n is odd, n² is also odd. Therefore r is true.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.r.b: The direction of the logic is right. But it assumed that 'odd×odd=odd' is already known. Look at whether that fact was shown separately.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.o.c: Hajun: If n is odd, then n=2k+1 (k is an integer) and n²=2(2k²+2k)+1 is odd. Therefore r is true.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.explain: Seoa only checked some cases, so it is not a proof. Hajun showed the contrapositive 'If n is odd, then n² is also odd' directly with 2k+1. Jiyu showed the same contrapositive by relying on the fact 'odd×odd=odd'. If you accept that fact, or show it by expanding (2k+1)(2m+1), the proof is complete.
y-m-48-09.s.s1.acc.0: Jiyu's (b) solution uses the same logic as Hajun (negating the conclusion negates the hypothesis) as long as you accept 'odd×odd=odd' as an already known fact. If that fact is shown separately, it is more complete.

y-m-48-09.s.s2.model.0: r and 'If n is odd, then n² is also odd' have the same truth value (the contrapositive), so we can show this one. An odd number can be written as 2k+1 for some integer k, so if we square it and see whether it becomes the form 2×(integer)+1, we can tell whether n² is odd.

y-m-48-09.s.s3.o.b: If n³ is even, then n is even

y-m-48-10.title: Make a subset that satisfies all the conditions
y-m-48-10.topic: Number of subsets and making sets that fit conditions
y-m-48-10.goal: Split into cases by whether elements are included to count the subsets that fit the conditions, and explain how the count changes when one more condition is added.
y-m-48-10.material: We make a subset X of the universal set S={1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. The conditions are as follows. (가) 1 is an element of X. (나) 3 and 5 are not in X together (only one of them is in it, or neither is). Condition (다) will be added later.
